extracted.intended_audience: students and teachers of mathematics; general problem-solvers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative criteria for heuristic problem solving in mathematics: how to think, choose notation, vary and analyze problems, and teach/problem-solve effectively. Emphasis is on general procedures (analysis/synthesis), notation choices, and pedagogical cautions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim at general features independent of subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘we should aim at general features, independent of the subject matter of the problem.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heuristic has 'practical' aims; understanding mental operations useful in solving problems can influence teaching, especially mathematics instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: List as mental operations useful in solving problems
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Our list is, in fact, a list of mental operations typically useful in solving problems; the questions and suggestions listed hint at such operations.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some operations are expanded or illustrated in other parts of the work; cross-reference the dictionary articles whose titles are the first sentences of the paragraphs for more detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refer to dictionary articles for deeper guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: For additional information about particular questions and suggestions of the list, the reader should refer to those fifteen articles of the Dictionary whose titles are the first sentences of the fifteen paragraphs of the list.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To find explanation of a suggestion, look up the article titled with the paragraph's first words (example: 'Go back to definitions' is under the paragraph beginning 'COULD YOU RESTATE THE PROBLEM?').

rubrics_metrics.name: Study PROGRESS AND ACHIEVEMENT early
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘What is essential to PROGRESS AND ACHIEVEMENT in solving problems?’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article discussing progress and achievement should be read fairly early; understanding how progress feels (elation, depression) is important to problem work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variation of the problem is essential
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘VARIATION OF THE PROBLEM is essential to our work.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vary the problem by decomposing and recombining its elements, returning to definitions, or using generalization, specialization, and analogy; variation may lead to auxiliary elements or to discovery of an auxiliary problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish problems to-find vs problems to-prove
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘We have to distinguish carefully between two kinds of problems, PROBLEMS TO FIND, PROBLEMS TO PROVE.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The provided list is specially adapted to 'problems-to-find' and should be revised for 'problems-to-prove' (different questions/suggestions apply).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use suitable notation and geometrical figures
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘In all sorts of problems, but especially in mathematical problems which are not too simple, suitable NOTATION and geometrical FIGURES are a great and often indispensable help.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Well-chosen notation and clear figures can be essential; choose notation early to avoid confusion and aid understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heuristic reasoning is provisional—examine your guess
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Provisional, merely plausible HEURISTIC REASONING is important in discovering the solution, but you should not take it for a proof; you must guess, but also EXAMINE YOUR GUESS.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heuristic arguments help find solutions but must be followed by examination and proof; see discussion in SIGNS OF PROGRESS.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude overly subtle/technical points from first exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Some aspects of problem solving are omitted or only briefly treated in this exposition when they appear too subtle, technical, or controversial for a first short exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This justifies a focus on more broadly useful procedures in an introductory treatment; advanced or controversial matters can be deferred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include psychological aspects but treat briefly
rubrics_metrics.description: There are only two articles predominantly devoted to psychological aspects (DETERMINATION, HOPE, SUCCESS, SUBCONSCIENT WORK); other psychological remarks are incidental.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Psychological factors matter but are not the primary focus here; see WORKING BACKWARDS for incidental remarks on animal psychology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heuristic aims at generality across problem types
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Heuristic aims at generality, at the study of procedures which are independent of the subject-matter and apply to all sorts of problems.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although examples quoted are almost exclusively elementary mathematical problems, the procedures are intended to be general and applicable beyond mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use dialogues/mental discourse as a model of problem thinking
rubrics_metrics.description: Dialogues between teacher and students may serve as models to the teacher and to the problem-solver working alone; describe thinking as 'mental discourse' or a conversation with oneself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These dialogues show progress of the solution; problem-solvers can emulate that self-questioning progression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose notation carefully; initial time is repaid
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘An important step in solving a problem is to choose the notation. It should be done carefully. The time we spend now on choosing the notation may be well repaid by the time we save later by avoiding hesitation and confusion.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choosing notation forces you to think of the problem's elements and can contribute essentially to understanding the problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good notation: unambiguous, pregnant, easy to remember
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘A good notation should be unambiguous, pregnant, easy to remember; it should avoid harmful second meanings, and take advantage of useful second meanings; the order and connection of signs should suggest the order and connection of things.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for notation that suggests relations among objects and is memorable; avoid ambiguous or misleading symbol choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using same symbol for different objects in same inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘It is inadmissible that the same symbol denote two different objects in the same inquiry.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Within one problem, do not reuse a symbol for different magnitudes; you may reuse letters in different problems but be consistent within a problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer one sign per object; multiple signs require care
rubrics_metrics.description: Although it's forbidden to use the same symbol for different objects, it is not forbidden to use different symbols for the same object. Usually it is better to use just one sign for one object, and in no case should several signs be used wantonly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple notations for the same object can be used but only with particular care to avoid confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signs should be easy to recognize and recall (use initials carefully)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘A good sign should be easy to remember and easy to recognize; the sign should immediately remind us of the object and the object of the sign.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using initials (r for rate, t for time, V for volume) is a simple device, but constraints (like letter already taken) may require alternative choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notation can shape conception through ordering and alphabets
rubrics_metrics.description: Notation ordering (letters near each other in the alphabet) and use of different alphabets for categories (Roman capitals for points, small Roman for lines, small Greek for angles) helps indicate relationships and categories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose letters so their order and alphabet suggest roles (e.g., a,b,c for given constants; x,y,z for variables) and use corresponding letters (A and a) to show linked objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose letters to connote roles and relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use letters to indicate nature/connection of elements (example: a,b as constants; x,y as variables; a precedes b as x precedes y suggesting a : b = x : y).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thoughtful choice of letters can encode relations and reduce later cognitive load.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer 'pregnant' (expressive) notation
rubrics_metrics.description: A notation expressing more than another may be termed more pregnant; modern notation for triangle similitude is more pregnant and allows deriving consequences without a figure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select notation that reflects order and connection of things and can serve as basis for more consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect traditional second meanings of symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain letters have traditional meanings (e for base of natural logarithms, i for imaginary unit, π for circumference/diameter) and it is on the whole better to use such symbols only in their traditional meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid reassigning widely-rooted symbols to new meanings as harmful second meanings can mislead; beginners are less troubled but experts can be misled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use helpful secondary meanings and standing notation with tact
rubrics_metrics.description: Second meanings of symbols can be helpful if used with tact; standing notation used on several occasions may assist in recalling formerly used procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful to separate the present primary meaning from former secondary meanings when reusing standing notation in a different sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance reasons and use experience/taste in choosing notation
rubrics_metrics.description: When choosing between two notations, multiple reasons may speak for each; we need experience and taste to choose the more suitable notation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know the advantages and disadvantages discussed and have good reasons for your choice rather than arbitrary selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach notation benefits to students; provide experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Students may resist new notation as a memory burden; the teacher's task is to give them ample opportunity to convince themselves by experience that mathematical notation assists the mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommend checking formulas by extensive discussion of their properties as an instructive exercise (see CAN YOU CHECK THE RESULT?).

rubrics_metrics.name: Analysis: assume the desired result and work backwards
rubrics_metrics.description: In analysis, we start from what is required, take it for granted, and draw consequences from it until we reach a point that we can use as starting point in synthesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysis (solution backwards, regressive reasoning) is invention: assume the thing sought as existing and reduce it to something known.

rubrics_metrics.name: Synthesis: reverse analysis and construct the solution
rubrics_metrics.description: In synthesis, reversing the process, we start from the point reached in analysis (a thing already known) and derive what preceded it until we arrive at what is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Synthesis (constructive solution, progressive reasoning) is execution: retrace the analytic steps forward to produce the solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure derivations are convertible (proviso for correctness)
rubrics_metrics.description: The paraphrase twice uses the important phrase 'provided that all our derivations are convertible.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convertibility of reductions is crucial: if analytic derivations are not reversible/convertible, conclusions from analysis may be invalid; see AUXILIARY PROBLEM for convertible reduction notion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use substitutions to simplify during analysis; synthesis executes computations
rubrics_metrics.description: Algebraic illustration: introduce advantageous substitutions in analysis to reduce the problem to a known solvable form; synthesis carries through the calculations retracing the steps of analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysis requires invention and finding substitutions; synthesis requires patience and attention in calculation to retrace and produce original unknowns.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Assume the problem as solved' is a provisional productive device
rubrics_metrics.description: To 'assume the problem as solved' means to assume provisionally that there exists an object satisfying the condition in order to start analysis; the assumption is harmless and natural.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assuming existence helps to visualize relations; if analysis leads to an impossibility, it shows the original problem has no solution. For 'problem to prove', assuming A as true invites drawing consequences even before proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pedantry; apply rules with mastery and judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Pedantry = applying a rule rigidly and unquestioningly; mastery = applying a rule with natural ease, judgment, and noticing cases where it fits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Questions and suggestions must be understood and learned by trial and error; do not apply them indiscriminately—use your own judgment and 'always use your own brains first.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize differences between practical and mathematical problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical problems have more complex, less sharply defined unknowns, data, and conditions than mathematical problems; they usually involve specialized scientific theories and empirical knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Despite differences in complexity and required knowledge, the fundamental motives and procedures of solution are essentially the same for both sorts of problems; practical problems may demand more experience but similar heuristic questions.
